title: Asking: question words and pronouns
intro: Every question word carries an accent — that accent is what makes it a question rather than a relative pronoun. Spanish also drops subject pronouns constantly, because the verb ending already says who is speaking; the pronouns below are for emphasis and for clearing up ambiguity.

entries.note: Asks for a definition or a thing. Unaccented que is the conjunction that.

ex.en: What do you want to drink?

entries.note: Takes a plural form when you expect more than one person.

ex.en: Who is coming to the dinner?
Where did you leave the keys?

entries.note: Spanish marks direction on the question word. English has to add a preposition at the end of the sentence.

ex.en: Where are you going in such a hurry?

entries.note: Two words with an accent asks the question; one word without answers it. A third form, el porqué, is the noun the reason.
Picks from a set. Before a noun Spanish prefers qué: ¿qué color? not ¿cuál color? But ¿cuál es tu nombre? — not ¿qué es tu nombre?

ex.en: There are two trains. Which one do we take?

entries.note: Asking someone to repeat themselves with ¿qué? is blunt; ¿cómo? is the polite one.
Agrees with the noun: cuánta agua, cuántas sillas.
Usually left out — hablo already means I speak. Say yo only to stress or contrast.

ex.es: Yo pago, tú invitas la próxima.
ex.en: I'll pay, you treat next time.

entries.note: With an accent it is the pronoun; without, tu means your. In Argentina and much of Central America vos replaces it.
Takes the same verb form as él and ella: usted tiene, not usted tienes. Abbreviated Ud.

ex.en: Do you already have your ticket?

entries.note: In Latin America this is the only plural you — formal and informal alike. Spain keeps a separate vosotros, which you can safely ignore.

ex.es: ¿Ustedes vienen en carro o en tren?
ex.en: Are you coming by car or by train?

entries.note: él with an accent is the pronoun; el without is the article the.

ex.es: Él cocina y ella lava los platos.
ex.en: He cooks and she washes the dishes.

entries.note: nosotras only if every one of you is female.
One man in the group and it goes back to ellos.
They sit before the verb, or stick onto the end of an infinitive or a command: quiero verte, llámame.

entries.en: to him, to her, to you (formal); to them
entries.note: The indirect object. Becomes se when lo or la follows: se lo dije.

ex.es: Le dije la verdad a mi jefa.
ex.en: I told my boss the truth.

ex.es: Les mandé un mensaje a los niños.
ex.en: I sent the children a message.

entries.en: my · your · his, her, your (formal), their
entries.note: su is genuinely ambiguous, so Spanish often clarifies: su casa de ella, or la casa de Marta.
Irregular one-word forms. Never con mí or con ti.

ex.en: Are you coming with me to the market?
